items.title: [Bug] Anthropic OAuth/Claude Max proxy path can misclassify full Hermes system prompt as extra-usage exhausted

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

Claude subscription/OAuth requests can return:

`HTTP 400: You're out of extra usage. Add more at claude.ai/settings/usage and keep going.`

...even when the Claude auth token is valid and minimal Anthropic Messages requests succeed.

On Tyler's macOS machine, the failure was not caused by the proxy itself, the OAuth token, or tool schemas alone. The trigger was the full Hermes-assembled system prompt on the Anthropic OAuth / Claude Max proxy path.

## Environment

- Hermes repo: `NousResearch/hermes-agent`
- Local branch where workaround was applied: `feat/context-budget-management`
- Local preserving commit: `5eeb76e5`
- Platform: macOS
- Provider runtime:
  - `provider: anthropic`
  - `api_mode: anthropic_messages`
  - `base_url: http://127.0.0.1:18801`
- Auth source: Claude Code / Claude subscription OAuth from `~/.claude/.credentials.json`
- Model: `claude-opus-4-6`

## What we verified

### 1. Proxy and auth were healthy

The local billing proxy on `127.0.0.1:18801` was restored and `/health` returned OK.

A direct minimal Anthropic SDK call through that same proxy succeeded:

```python
client.messages.create(
    model='claude-opus-4-6',
    max_tokens=8,
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Say OK'}],
)
```

Result: `OK`

So this was not simply "proxy down" or "OAuth token invalid".

### 2. The failure was prompt-shape sensitive

Using the same proxy, auth, and model:

- baseline user-only request: works
- Claude Code identity block only: works
- tools only: works
- full Hermes system block: fails with extra-usage 400

A local isolation script showed:

- `baseline` -> OK
- `cc_only` -> OK
- `tools_only` -> OK
- `soul_only` -> extra-usage 400
- `both_system` -> extra-usage 400
- `soul_plus_tools` -> extra-usage 400

Later inspection showed the failing "SOUL block" was actually a ~30k combined system block containing:

- `SOUL.md`
- memory guidance
- session-search guidance
- skill-management guidance
- platform/media instructions
- other prompt-builder text

So the actual trigger is the assembled Hermes system prompt on the OAuth path, not only the profile SOUL file.

### 3. A sanitizer workaround restores local end-to-end success

A local workaround in `agent/anthropic_adapter.py` rewrites several Hermes-specific prompt phrases before sending OAuth Anthropic requests.

After applying that patch, a local end-to-end Skippy turn through the resolved runtime bundle succeeded again:

```text
OK.
```

## Why this should be fixed upstream

This is not just a one-off local profile problem.

Hermes currently injects a large, Hermes-specific system prompt into the Anthropic OAuth / Claude Code path. On at least some Claude subscription / proxy routes, that prompt shape appears to get misclassified server-side as requiring extra usage, even though simple Anthropic Messages requests with the same auth work fine.

That makes the symptom look like a billing/auth outage when it is actually request-shape dependent.

## Proposed direction

At minimum, Hermes should defensively sanitize or slim the system prompt on the Anthropic OAuth path.

Possible fixes:

1. Keep a dedicated OAuth-path sanitizer in `agent/anthropic_adapter.py`
2. Reduce / rewrite the most brittle prompt-builder phrases before they reach the OAuth Anthropic path
3. Add a regression test covering:
   - direct minimal request succeeds
   - assembled system prompt does not regress into known brittle wording
4. Improve logging so this class of failure is distinguishable from genuine exhausted extra-usage state

## Notes

This may be related to the general symptom tracked in #6475, but this issue is narrower and includes a concrete root-cause finding:

- valid OAuth auth
- valid proxy path
- minimal request succeeds
- full Hermes system prompt fails
- sanitizer workaround restores success

items.title: [Bug]: Slack mention prefix (<@botid>) breaks is_command() slash-command detection
items.body:
## Bug Description

`MessageEvent.is_command()` at `gateway/platforms/base.py:693-695` checks `self.text.startswith("/")`. In Slack, when a user addresses the bot with a mention (`<@U0AN0V870R1> /sethome`), the raw event text arrives prefixed with the mention token and fails the `startswith("/")` check — so the command is routed to the agent as ordinary conversational text instead of being handled by the command dispatcher.

In practice: `@Vera /sethome` in a Slack channel is silently ignored as a command; only `/sethome` typed without the mention (DM or plain channel message) actually fires `_handle_set_home_command`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Hermes with Slack adapter, bot installed in a channel
2. In the channel, type `@<bot> /sethome`
3. Observe: nothing happens command-side. The agent receives the message as normal text and typically delegates / replies conversationally.
4. In a DM to the bot (no mention prefix), type `/sethome` — works as expected.

## Expected Behavior

Slash commands should work whether or not the user prefixes with a bot mention. The mention prefix is a natural Slack convention for addressing bots in shared channels and shouldn't silently disable the command path.

## Actual Behavior

`is_command()` returns `False` for `"<@U...> /sethome"` because the text doesn't start with `/`. The message falls through to normal message handling and is delivered to the agent verbatim.

## Root Cause

`gateway/platforms/base.py`:

```python
def is_command(self) -> bool:
    """Check if this is a command message (e.g., /new, /reset)."""
    return self.text.startswith("/")
```

No mention-strip happens before this check.

Note: `gateway/platforms/slack.py:1044` does perform a mention-strip (`text = text.replace(f"<@{bot_uid}>", "").strip()`) but only inside `_handle_message_event` for the normal message path, AFTER the event is already constructed. The MessageEvent reaches `is_command()` via other code paths (e.g., the command dispatch in `run.py:3018-3019` for `/sethome`) with the unstripped text.

## Proposed Fix

Either:

**Option A (preferred):** Strip a leading `<@botid>` token inside `is_command()` / `get_command()` so detection is robust regardless of which code path produces the MessageEvent:

```python
def is_command(self) -> bool:
    text = self.text.lstrip()
    # Strip Slack mention prefix if present (e.g., "<@U0123> /sethome")
    import re
    text = re.sub(r"^<@[A-Z0-9]+>\s*", "", text)
    return text.startswith("/")
```

(and apply the same strip in `get_command()` / `get_command_args()` so the extracted command name is clean).

**Option B:** Normalize `self.text` at MessageEvent construction in `slack.py` — strip mention there, before handing off to dispatch. Risk: other adapters would need their own normalization and drift over time.

## Affected Component

Gateway (base MessageEvent + Slack adapter interaction)

## Messaging Platform

Slack (primarily; any platform that prefixes user messages with a mention token could hit this)

## Hermes Version

v0.9.0 (verified on pod — code at `/opt/hermes/gateway/platforms/base.py:693`)

## Related

- Discord `/sethome` config-write bug: #6447
- WhatsApp `/sethome` persistence: #9220

items.title: [Feature]: Cron job 'created' notification should respect thread_ts of originating message
items.body:
## Problem

When a user in a Slack thread asks the agent to schedule a cron job, the confirmation message Hermes posts ("📁 Cron job created: `<id>` — will run ...") is always top-level in the channel, never a reply in the originating thread. This breaks thread discipline and surfaces internal-looking scheduling chatter at channel top-level where non-participants see it out of context.

## Expected Behavior

If the cron creation was triggered by a message in a thread (`thread_ts` present on the originating MessageEvent), the creation notification should reply in the same thread.

If the cron creation came from a top-level message, DM, or cronjob console, the notification can stay top-level (current behavior).

## Actual Behavior

The built-in "cron job created" notification ignores `thread_ts` and is posted as a top-level message on the channel.

## Context / Motivation

In our deployment the agent operates in shared channels with strict thread discipline (thread-originated requests → thread-only replies). A cron creation triggered from a thread conversation landing top-level is visually indistinguishable from the agent "escaping" the thread for an unauthorized broadcast. It also breaks the common UX expectation that an action taken in a thread reports back in that thread.

Concrete example: a non-owner asked the agent for a weekly digest in a thread; the agent created a cron job, and the "📁 Cron job created..." confirmation landed as a top-level channel message, visible to everyone in the channel rather than scoped to the thread participants.

## Proposed Fix

Wherever the cron creation notification is produced (Slack adapter / cron tool return path), propagate the originating `thread_ts` through to the notification send. Slack's `chat.postMessage` accepts `thread_ts`; the adapter already supports it for other responses.

Signature sketch:

```python
await adapter.send(
    chat_id=source.chat_id,
    text=f"📁 Cron job created: `{job_id}` ...",
    thread_ts=source.thread_ts,   # <-- propagate this
)
```

The same fix likely applies to the "cron job updated" / "cron job deleted" confirmations.

## Affected Component

Gateway — cron tool / Slack adapter notification path

## Messaging Platform

Slack (primarily; Discord thread-like behavior may benefit similarly)

## Hermes Version

v0.9.0

## Related

- #8866 — cron delivery target hijacking (different symptom, same "cron + routing state" family)

items.title: [Feature]: Route Slack reaction_added events to the agent so emoji reactions are observable
items.body:
## Problem

The Slack adapter does not route `reaction_added` (or `reaction_removed`) events to the agent. Hermes **emits** reactions outbound (👀 / ✅ lifecycle ack at `gateway/platforms/slack.py:509-539`, 1131-1138), but it has no code path that consumes inbound reaction events — they fall through to slack_bolt's default unhandled-request handler.

This makes emoji reactions "silent" from the agent's perspective: an operator or owner can ✅ a proposal message, but the agent has no way to observe that, so any prompt-layer rule that treats a ✅ as a confirmation signal is unenforceable without an accompanying text message.

## Expected Behavior

If the Slack app is subscribed to `reaction_added` (already common; required anyway for #6572's suppression fix not to be needed), Hermes should register a handler that converts the event into an internal event/callback the agent can consume — e.g., a `ReactionEvent` that reaches the current session similar to how `MessageEvent` does. At minimum: emit a structured event with the reacting user's Slack user_id, the target message's ts + channel, and the reaction name, so prompt-layer rules and skills can act on it.

## Actual Behavior

`gateway/platforms/slack.py:179-196` registers exactly four Slack Bolt handlers: `message`, `app_mention`, `assistant_thread_started`, `assistant_thread_context_changed`. Nothing listens for `reaction_added`. Grep across the repo confirms no `ReactionEvent` concept exists for Slack (Feishu has `_handle_reaction_event` at `gateway/platforms/feishu.py:1835`, but that's platform-local).

## Use Case / Motivation

We use Slack reactions (specifically ✅) as a lightweight "Owner approved" signal for proposed behavior/config changes. Our prompt-layer rule says a ✅ from an Owner authorizes implementation. Without event routing, that rule is decorative — the agent cannot see the ✅ unless the Owner also posts a text message. We've had to degrade the rule to "✅ only counts if accompanied by a text reference to it," which is awkward UX for Owners used to reacting as a primary signal.

Broader value: reactions are a natural, low-friction confirmation/approval signal in Slack. Many agent-driven workflows (approvals, acknowledgements, snooze/archive commands, "mark as handled") could use them once they're observable.

## Proposed Fix

Add a `reaction_added` (and `reaction_removed`) handler in `gateway/platforms/slack.py` that constructs an internal event and dispatches it to the active session, if any. Shape sketch:

```python
@self._app.event("reaction_added")
async def handle_reaction_added(event, say):
    reaction_event = ReactionEvent(
        platform=Platform.SLACK,
        reaction=event["reaction"],              # e.g. "white_check_mark"
        user_id=event["user"],                   # reacting user's Slack ID
        channel_id=event["item"]["channel"],
        message_ts=event["item"]["ts"],
        timestamp=datetime.fromtimestamp(float(event["event_ts"])),
    )
    await self._dispatch_reaction(reaction_event)
```

Open design questions for maintainers:
- Should reactions on any visible message dispatch, or only reactions on messages the bot itself sent / was mentioned in?
- How should this interact with the existing thread/session routing — tie to the message's thread_ts if the reacted message is in a thread?
- What subset of reactions should trigger agent wake-up vs be logged and ignored?

Happy to help prototype.

## Affected Component

Gateway — Slack adapter

## Messaging Platform

Slack (this issue). A parallel Discord issue may exist — Discord reactions work differently and may already have partial support.

## Hermes Version

v0.9.0

## Related

- #6572 — Slack `reaction_added` generates slack_bolt WARNING spam (proposed fix is a catch-all no-op handler; PR #6580). That fix silences the warnings but explicitly does NOT route events to the agent, so it doesn't address this issue.
- #8372 — configurable reactions toggle (outbound reactions, different angle)

items.title: Cron job creation should reconstruct DM origin from HERMES_SESSION_KEY when session vars are missing
items.body:
## Bug description

When a cron job is created from a Weixin DM (and likely other DM platforms), the cron tool can persist:

```json
{
  "deliver": "origin",
  "origin": null
}
```

Even when the gateway session still has a valid `HERMES_SESSION_KEY` like:

```text
agent:main:weixin:dm:<chat_id>
```

This makes `deliver=origin` fragile: if explicit session platform/chat env vars are missing in the worker thread, the cron tool drops the origin metadata instead of reconstructing it from the session key.

## Why this is a separate bug from the existing issues

There are already open issues/PRs around cron delivery:

- `#8848` / `#9193`: `deliver=origin` fallback missing `weixin`/`feishu`/`wecom`
- `#9354` / `#10227`: gateway worker threads lose session contextvars, so cron creation may not see `HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM` / `HERMES_SESSION_CHAT_ID`

Those are real, but the cron tool still has a robustness gap of its own:

- `tools/cronjob_tools.py::_origin_from_env()` only trusts explicit `HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM` + `HERMES_SESSION_CHAT_ID`
- if those are unavailable, it returns `None`
- it does **not** attempt to reconstruct DM origin from `HERMES_SESSION_KEY`, even though the DM session key format is deterministic and reversible

So even with the broader gateway/contextvars fixes pending, the cron tool is currently less defensive than it could be.

## Reproduction

1. Start from a Weixin DM session.
2. Ensure `HERMES_SESSION_KEY=agent:main:weixin:dm:<chat_id>` is present.
3. Create a cron job through the cron tool.
4. In the execution path where `HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM` / `HERMES_SESSION_CHAT_ID` are missing, inspect `~/.hermes/cron/jobs.json`.
5. The created job is stored with:
   - `deliver: "origin"`
   - `origin: null`

## Expected behavior

If explicit session vars are unavailable, `_origin_from_env()` should fall back to parsing DM `HERMES_SESSION_KEY` values of the form:

```text
agent:main:<platform>:dm:<chat_id>[:<thread_id>]
```

and reconstruct:

```json
{
  "platform": "weixin",
  "chat_id": "...",
  "thread_id": null
}
```

## Suggested fix

In `tools/cronjob_tools.py`, make `_origin_from_env()`:

1. first read `HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM` / `HERMES_SESSION_CHAT_ID` as it does today
2. if missing, read `HERMES_SESSION_KEY`
3. if the key matches DM format, reconstruct origin from it

Pseudo-shape:

```python
session_key = get_session_env("HERMES_SESSION_KEY")
parts = session_key.split(":") if session_key else []
if len(parts) >= 5 and parts[0] == "agent" and parts[1] == "main" and parts[3] == "dm":
    return {
        "platform": parts[2],
        "chat_id": parts[4],
        "thread_id": parts[5] if len(parts) >= 6 else None,
    }
```

## Why this helps

This does not replace the gateway-side context propagation fix, but it makes cron creation much more resilient:

- DM-origin cron jobs stop depending on a single env propagation path
- origin metadata is still preserved when the session key is available
- `deliver=origin` becomes safer for Weixin/Telegram/other DM platforms

## Regression test ideas

Add tests for:

1. explicit platform/chat vars still win when present
2. Weixin DM session key reconstructs `platform=weixin`, `chat_id=<id>`, `thread_id=None`
3. DM session key with thread id reconstructs the thread id correctly

items.title: [Bug]: profile import can clobber an existing profile when archive root name differs from --name

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Summary
`import_profile(..., name="foo")` can overwrite and rename an existing profile if the archive's top-level directory is a different existing profile name.

## Affected code
- `hermes_cli/profiles.py:887-931`
- `tests/hermes_cli/test_profiles.py` (currently covers same-name collisions and traversal, but not conflicting archive top-level names)

## Why this is a bug
`import_profile()` only checks whether the target destination (`get_profile_dir(inferred_name)`) already exists.

It does **not** check whether the archive's extracted top-level directory already exists under `profiles/`. `_safe_extract_profile_archive()` then writes into that existing directory with `exist_ok=True`, and the final rename step moves that pre-existing directory to the requested name.

That means importing `bar.tar.gz` as `foo` can silently mutate/consume an existing `bar` profile.

## Minimal reproduction
```python
import io, os, tarfile, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from hermes_cli.profiles import import_profile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as td:
    root = Path(td) / ".hermes"
    os.environ["HERMES_HOME"] = str(root)
    profiles = root / "profiles"
    profiles.mkdir(parents=True)

    # Existing profile that should remain untouched.
    existing = profiles / "bar"
    existing.mkdir()
    (existing / "keep.txt").write_text("original-bar")

    # Archive top-level dir is bar/, but import target is foo.
    archive = Path(td) / "bar.tar.gz"
    with tarfile.open(archive, "w:gz") as tf:
        payload = b"new-from-archive"
        info = tarfile.TarInfo("bar/new.txt")
        info.size = len(payload)
        tf.addfile(info, io.BytesIO(payload))

    import_profile(str(archive), name="foo")
```

Actual result after import:
- `profiles/bar` disappears
- `profiles/foo/keep.txt` still contains the old `bar` content
- `profiles/foo/new.txt` contains imported data

Expected result:
- abort before extraction/rename with a collision error, or extract into an isolated temp dir and only move into place after validating both names
- existing `bar` profile must remain untouched

## Impact
This is destructive profile management behavior. A user importing a backup under a new name can accidentally corrupt or rename an unrelated existing profile.

## Suggested investigation
- inspect archive top-level names before extraction and reject when any extracted root collides with an existing profile that is not the requested destination
- or extract into a temp dir first, then move the validated result into `profile_dir`
- add a regression test to `tests/hermes_cli/test_profiles.py` for "archive top-level collides with existing profile while --name points elsewhere"

items.body:
## Summary

Add [Brave Search API](https://brave.com/search/api/) as a first-class web search backend in hermes-agent, alongside existing providers (Firecrawl, Parallel, Tavily, Exa).

## Motivation

Brave Search is one of the most accessible and cost-effective search APIs available:
- Generous free tier with monthly trial credits
- Well-documented REST API with structured JSON responses
- Supports web search, query autosuggest, and AI-grounded answers with citations
- Privacy-focused — no tracking, no user profiling
- Already widely adopted (used by OmniRoute as `brave-search` provider)

## Proposed Integration

### 1. New tool file: `tools/brave_search_tool.py`

Three tools registered via the standard `registry.register()` pattern:

#### `brave_search` — Web Search
- Endpoint: `GET https://api.search.brave.com/res/v1/web/search`
- Auth: `X-Subscription-Token` header with `BRAVE_API_KEY` or `BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY`
- Parameters:
  - `query` (required) — search query, supports operators: `site:`, `"exact phrase"`, `-exclude`
  - `count` (1-20, default 10)
  - `country` (2-letter code, default `us`)
  - `freshness` — `pd` (24h), `pw` (7d), `pm` (31d), `py` (1y)
  - `extra_snippets` (bool) — up to 5 extra excerpts per result
  - `summary` (bool) — fetch Brave AI summarizer result

**Response format (standardized):**
```json
{
  "query": "...",
  "results": [
    {
      "title": "...",
      "url": "https://...",
      "description": "...",
      "extra_snippets": ["..."]
    }
  ],
  "ai_summary": "..."
}
```

#### `brave_suggest` — Query Autosuggest
- Endpoint: `GET https://api.search.brave.com/res/v1/suggest/search`
- Parameters: `query`, `count` (1-10), `country`, `rich` (metadata)
- Response: `{"query": "...", "suggestions": ["..."]}`

#### `brave_answers` — AI-Grounded Answers
- Endpoint: `POST https://api.search.brave.com/res/v1/chat/completions`
- Auth: `BRAVE_ANSWERS_API_KEY` (may differ from search key)
- Body: OpenAI-compatible chat format with `model: "brave"`
- Extra params: `enable_citations`, `enable_research` (multi-search deep mode)
- Parses `<citation>...</citation>` tags to extract sources

**Response format:**
```json
{
  "answer": "...",
  "sources": [
    {"url": "...", "title": "...", "snippet": "..."}
  ],
  "tokens": 123
}
```

### 2. Backend integration in `web_tools.py`

Add `"brave"` to:
- `_get_backend()` — valid configured backend name
- `_is_backend_available()` — check for `BRAVE_API_KEY` or `BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY`
- `backend_candidates` fallback list (priority: after firecrawl, before parallel)
- `_web_requires_env()` — include `BRAVE_API_KEY`, `BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY`

### 3. Toolset updates in `toolsets.py`

Add `brave_search` and `brave_answers` to:
- `"web"` toolset: `["web_search", "web_extract", "brave_search", "brave_answers"]`
- `"search"` toolset: `["web_search", "brave_search", "brave_answers"]`

### 4. Config updates in `hermes_cli/config.py`

Add to `OPTIONAL_ENV_VARS`:
```python
"BRAVE_API_KEY": {
    "description": "Brave Search API key (web search)",
    "prompt": "Brave Search API Key",
    "url": "https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com",
    "category": "tool",
}
"BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY": {
    "description": "Brave Search API key (explicit, overrides BRAVE_API_KEY)",
    "prompt": "Brave Search API Key",
    "url": "https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com",
    "category": "tool",
}
"BRAVE_ANSWERS_API_KEY": {
    "description": "Brave AI Answers API key (requires paid plan)",
    "prompt": "Brave Answers API Key",
    "url": "https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com",
    "category": "tool",
}
```

Add `"brave"` to the web backend selector in `hermes tools` setup.

### 5. Tool discovery in `model_tools.py`

Add `"tools.brave_search_tool"` to the `_modules` list in `_discover_tools()`.

## Existing Web Search Providers (for reference)

| Provider | Search | Extract | Crawl | Env Var |
|----------|--------|---------|-------|---------|
| Firecrawl | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` |
| Parallel | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | `PARALLEL_API_KEY` |
| Tavily | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | `TAVILY_API_KEY` |
| Exa | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | `EXA_API_KEY` |
| **Brave** | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | `BRAVE_API_KEY` |

items.title: [Bug]: GitHub Copilot ACP mode fails due to deprecated gh-copilot CLI, and GitHub Models endpoint hits 8K token limit (HTTP 413)
items.body:
### Bug Description

### Describe the bug
I encountered two blocking issues when trying to use GitHub Copilot as the inference provider for Hermes. First, the official ACP mode is broken because GitHub deprecated the underlying CLI extension. Second, trying to use the GitHub Models API as a workaround fails because Hermes' system prompt exceeds GitHub's hard 8000 token limit.

---

### Issue 1: GitHub Copilot ACP Mode is Broken (Upstream Deprecation)
When running `hermes setup` and selecting `(○) GitHub Copilot ACP (spawns copilot --acp --stdio)`, Hermes fails to start and hangs/errors out.

**Root Cause:**
If you manually test the underlying command in the terminal (`gh copilot explain "test"`), GitHub now returns a deprecation error and refuses to execute:
> The gh-copilot extension has been deprecated in favor of the newer GitHub Copilot CLI.
> For more information, visit:
> - Copilot CLI: https://github.com/github/copilot-cli
> - Deprecation announcement: https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-25-upcoming-deprecation-of-gh-copilot-cli-extension
> No commands will be executed.

**Impact:** The current ACP mode in Hermes relies on a disabled GitHub extension and is completely unusable.

---

### Issue 2: GitHub Models Endpoint hits HTTP 413 (8000 Token Limit)
Since ACP mode is dead, I tried using the official GitHub Models API as a `Custom endpoint`:
- **Base URL:** `https://models.inference.ai.azure.com`
- **Provider:** `custom`
- **API Key:** A valid Fine-grained PAT with `Models Read-only` permission.

Authentication (`HTTP 401`) passes, but Hermes immediately crashes on the first prompt with an `HTTP 413` error:
```text
⚠️  API call failed (attempt 1/3): APIStatusError [HTTP 413]
   🔌 Provider: custom  Model: gpt-4o
   🌐 Endpoint: [https://models.inference.ai.azure.com](https://models.inference.ai.azure.com)
   📝 Error: HTTP 413: Request body too large for gpt-4o model. Max size: 8000 tokens.

### Steps to Reproduce

Scenario 1: Using the built-in GitHub Copilot ACP mode

In a Linux environment, log in to the gh CLI using an account with an active GitHub Copilot Student subscription.

Install the extension: gh extension install github/gh-copilot.

Run hermes setup and select (●) GitHub Copilot ACP (spawns copilot --acp --stdio) as the provider.

Execute hermes and attempt to initialize a conversation.

Scenario 2: Using the GitHub Models API as a Custom Endpoint

Generate a Fine-grained PAT on GitHub with Models Read-only account permissions.

Run hermes setup and select Custom endpoint.

Set Base URL to https://models.inference.ai.azure.com, set Model to gpt-4o-mini, and provide the PAT as the API key.

Launch hermes and send an initial prompt (e.g., "Hello").

### Expected Behavior

For Scenario 1: Hermes should successfully communicate with the gh-copilot extension via ACP mode, complete initialization, and respond to prompts.

For Scenario 2: Since the PAT is valid and gpt-4o-mini theoretically supports a 128k context window, Hermes should be able to load its system prompt and proceed with the task.

### Actual Behavior

Both official/workaround integration paths fail due to upstream architectural constraints:

ACP Mode Failure (Scenario 1):
The hermes agent hangs or returns an HTTP 403. Investigation reveals that GitHub has officially deprecated the gh-copilot extension. Manually running the command in the terminal confirms the refusal to execute:

"The gh-copilot extension has been deprecated in favor of the newer GitHub Copilot CLI... No commands will be executed."
Because the underlying dependency is disabled, the ACP communication bridge in Hermes is broken.

Payload Limit Conflict (Scenario 2):
Authentication succeeds, but the first request immediately fails with an HTTP 413 (Payload Too Large) error.
Despite gpt-4o-mini supporting 128k context, the GitHub Models free tier (via Azure) enforces a strict 8000 token limit per request. Because Hermes initializes with an extensive System Prompt (containing environment instructions, terminal tool definitions, etc.), the payload size instantly exceeds the 8k threshold, making this endpoint incompatible with the agent.

Full Error Output (Scenario 2)
⚠️  API call failed (attempt 1/3): APIStatusError [HTTP 413]
   🔌 Provider: custom  Model: gpt-4o-mini
   🌐 Endpoint: https://models.inference.ai.azure.com
   📝 Error: HTTP 413: Request body too large for gpt-4o-mini model. Max size: 8000 tokens.
   📋 Details: {'code': 'tokens_limit_reached', 'message': 'Request body too large for gpt-4o-mini model. Max size: 8000 tokens.'}

❌ Payload too large and cannot compress further.

_No response_

Error: HTTP 413 (Request body too large)

Root Cause: GitHub Models (Azure) enforces a hard 8000 token limit per request. The Hermes system prompt (including tools and environment context) is larger than 8k tokens, causing an immediate failure.

ACP Failure: gh-copilot extension is deprecated by GitHub and returns a non-zero exit code with a deprecation message, preventing Hermes from establishing a connection.
```

items.title: feat(cron): add script_skip_if_empty to skip LLM when script returns empty output

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Problem

Currently, cron jobs with a `script` field always invoke the LLM after the script runs — even when the script returns empty output (meaning there is nothing to report). This wastes LLM calls and can produce noisy "no output" deliveries.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `script_skip_if_empty` field to cron jobs. When set to `true`, if the script exits zero with empty stdout, the scheduler skips the LLM invocation entirely and suppresses delivery.

### Behavior

| Script result | `script_skip_if_empty=false` (default) | `script_skip_if_empty=true` |
|---|---|---|
| Exit non-zero | Error injected into prompt, LLM called | Same |
| Exit zero + empty stdout | "No output" notice injected, LLM called | **Skip LLM silently, no delivery** |
| Exit zero + non-empty stdout | Output injected, LLM called | Same |

### Example Use Case

```python
# check_github.py — exits 0 with output only when there are new commits
import subprocess, sys
result = subprocess.run(["git", "fetch", "origin"], capture_output=True)
result = subprocess.run(["git", "log", "HEAD..origin/main", "--oneline"], capture_output=True)
if result.stdout.strip():
    print(result.stdout.strip())
    sys.exit(0)
# no new commits — silent skip
```

```python
cronjob(
    action="create",
    prompt="Summarize the new commits below.",
    schedule="every 1h",
    script="check_github.py",
    script_skip_if_empty=True,
)
```

## Implementation

- `cron/jobs.py`: `create_job()` gains `script_skip_if_empty: bool = False` parameter, stored in job dict
- `cron/scheduler.py`: `run_job()` checks the flag; if script exits zero with empty output and flag is true, returns early (success, no LLM call)
- `tools/cronjob_tools.py`: `cronjob()` tool gains `script_skip_if_empty` param on create/update
- Tests and docs included

## Alternatives Considered

A separate `precheck` field was considered but rejected — it would duplicate the existing `script` field's execution model. Adding a boolean flag to `script` is simpler and avoids a redundant mechanism.

---

Feature branch: `jneeee/feat/cron-precheck-skip-llm`

items.title: [Feature]: Add a visible live activity indicator (spinner/progress bar) to TUI mode
items.body:
## Problem or Use Case

I frequently use Hermes Agent's TUI mode on a remote server, connecting via SSH. When Hermes is processing a request (e.g., calling tools, waiting for LLM response), there is no consistently visible live activity indicator in the TUI. Although a timestamp sometimes updates dynamically, this behavior is inconsistent — often the screen appears completely static while Hermes is still working.

This becomes a real problem when the SSH connection is unstable. When the TUI goes quiet, I cannot tell whether:
1. Hermes is still actively processing (working fine, just slow), or
2. The network connection has silently dropped, and I'm staring at a stale terminal

This ambiguity leads to wasted time — either waiting too long on a dead connection, or killing and restarting a session that was actually still running.

The TUI is excellent and I genuinely prefer using it over gateway channels (WeChat, Telegram, etc.) when I'm at my computer. A reliable activity indicator would make the TUI significantly more trustworthy for remote usage.

## Proposed Solution

Add a persistent, visually obvious live activity indicator to the TUI that is visible whenever Hermes is actively processing. For example:

- A **spinning animation** (e.g., ⠋⠙⠹⠸⠼⠴⠦⠧⠇⠏) or an **oscillating progress bar** (e.g., `[=====>    ]`) displayed in the status area
- The indicator should be active during any waiting state: LLM inference, tool execution, network requests, etc.
- It should stop/change only when Hermes is truly idle and waiting for user input

### Expected behavior

| State | TUI Display |
|---|---|
| Waiting for user input | Static prompt, no spinner |
| LLM is generating | Spinner active + "Thinking..." |
| Tool is executing | Spinner active + "Running tool: <name>..." |
| Network issue (no response) | Spinner keeps going — user knows connection may be dead |

This gives the user an immediate visual cue: **if the spinner is moving, Hermes is alive; if it freezes, the network likely dropped.**

## Alternatives Considered

- **Periodic timestamp update**: Already partially exists but is inconsistent and not visually prominent enough. A user watching a small timestamp change is much less intuitive than an animated spinner.
- **Heartbeat/beep on completion**: Would help detect when a long task finishes, but doesn't solve the "is it alive right now?" problem during the wait.
- **SSH keep-alive / terminal watchdog**: This is outside Hermes' scope and wouldn't distinguish between "Hermes is processing" vs "connection is dead."

A simple spinner or animated indicator is the most direct and universal solution.

## Feature Type

CLI improvement

## Scope

Small (single file or a few files, likely in the TUI rendering layer)

items.title: [Feature]: On-demand skill installation during setup + skill quality lifecycle

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Problem

Hermes currently bundles **79 skills** that are force-installed into `~/.hermes/skills/` on every CLI launch via `sync_skills()`. The setup wizard (`hermes setup`) has no skill selection step.

## The real problem: scattered, low-quality skills actively harm agent behavior

This is not just about "too many skills." Fragmented and low-quality bundled skills cause measurable damage to agent reliability:

### 1. Semantic collision — the agent picks the wrong skill
When 79 skills compete for the agent's attention, many have overlapping or vaguely related descriptions. The agent frequently loads a tangentially relevant skill instead of the correct one. Example: a user asking about "git workflow" might trigger `super-dev`, `hermes-workflow`, `github-toolkit`, or `skill-delegation-pattern` — each handles a different aspect, but the agent must guess which one actually applies. More skills = more guessing = more mistakes.

### 2. Context poisoning — loaded skill dumps irrelevant or misleading guidance
Once the agent loads a wrong or low-quality skill, its guidance becomes part of the working context. A thin, incomplete skill can steer the agent toward incorrect approaches. Unlike not having a skill (where the agent uses general knowledge), having a *bad* skill gives the agent false confidence — it follows the skill's instructions even when they are outdated, incomplete, or project-irrelevant.

### 3. Trigger dilution — high-quality skills get drowned out
Well-maintained toolkits like `github-toolkit` or `research-toolkit` have their semantic signal diluted by dozens of niche, rarely-used skills. The agent's skill-matching is probabilistic — a bloated skill list lowers the probability that the *correct* skill surfaces. Quality skills that should be easy to match become hard to find in the noise.

### 4. Skill auto-creation spiral
A bloated built-in skill list sets a precedent: "having lots of skills is normal." This encourages the agent to auto-create new skills for workflows it "discovers," many of which are redundant with existing built-in skills or low-quality clones. The result is a snowballing skill directory that gets harder to manage over time. (Recent fix removed the auto-creation prompt guidance, but the root environment is still permissive.)

### 5. Waste of finite context window
Every session loads the full skills index (~50KB for 79 skills) into the system prompt. This is a permanent tax on the context budget. For models with smaller context windows, or in long sessions where the context compressor is working hard, 50KB of irrelevant skill metadata is 50KB less room for actual conversation and tool results. Related: #4356, #10164.

### 6. Maintenance burden falls on users
When bundled skills are fragmented or low-quality, users are forced to become curators — manually aggregating skills, deleting ghosts, patching broken ones. This is exactly the wrong division of labor: the upstream distribution should ship a curated, high-quality set, not a kitchen-sink dump that users must clean up.

## Proposed Solution

### Phase 1: On-demand skill installation during `hermes setup`

Add a skill selection step to the setup wizard:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Skills Configuration                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                 │
│  Hermes ships with 79 bundled skills across     │
│  25 categories. You can install all of them or  │
│  select specific categories.                    │
│                                                 │
│  [1] Install all (default, current behavior)    │
│  [2] Select categories interactively            │
│  [3] Minimal — core skills only                 │
│                                                 │
│  You can always add/remove skills later with:   │
│  hermes skills install / hermes skills remove   │
│                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Category selection with checkboxes (like `hermes setup tools`):

```
  [✓] software-development  — super-dev, hermes-workflow, code-review-graph
  [✓] github-toolkit        — PR lifecycle, repo mgmt, code review
  [✓] research-toolkit      — arXiv, Semantic Scholar, blog monitoring
  [ ] email                 — himalaya email client
  [ ] social-media          — X/Twitter integration
  [ ] mlops                 — PEFT, vLLM, llama.cpp training/inference
  ...
```

**Core skills** (always installed, not optional):
- `task-dispatcher` — essential agent behavior
- `hermes-agent` — self-referential configuration guide

**Implementation approach**:
- Modify `sync_skills()` to support a category filter
- Store selection in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` under `skills.categories: [software-dev, github, ...]`
- On CLI launch, `sync_skills()` respects the category filter
- `hermes skills install` and `hermes skills remove` can override per-skill

### Phase 2: Skill quality tiers

Introduce metadata-based quality signaling:

```yaml
# In SKILL.md frontmatter
metadata:
  hermes:
    tier: core          # core | recommended | community | experimental
    maintainer: official  # official | community
    last_verified: 2026-04-15
```

- **core**: Must-have, always shown first, highest trigger priority
- **recommended**: Well-maintained, high utility, shown in setup suggestions
- **community**: Functional but less vetted, shown in `hermes skills browse`
- **experimental**: Untested, requires explicit opt-in

### Phase 3: Skill lifecycle management

- **Install**: On-demand during setup or via `hermes skills install`
- **Update**: `sync_skills()` respects installed set (current behavior, filtered)
- **Deprecate**: Skills can declare `deprecated: true` — agent warns user, suggests replacement
- **Remove**: `hermes skills remove <name>` — removes from disk and manifest, frees context

## Benefits

1. **Reduced system prompt**: Core-only installation could cut skills prompt from ~50KB to ~5-10KB
2. **Better agent accuracy**: Fewer skills = clearer semantic matching, fewer wrong-skill loads
3. **User agency**: Users choose what they need instead of getting everything
4. **Quality signal**: Tier system helps users and the agent distinguish reliable skills from experimental ones
5. **Incremental adoption**: New users start with a minimal, understandable skill set and add as needed

## Relationship to existing issues

- #4356 (Cap skills index): Addresses symptom. This proposal addresses root cause — fewer installed skills means a smaller index naturally.
- #10164 (Context-aware skills prompt): Complementary. Budget management is still needed even with fewer skills, but on-demand installation reduces the baseline.
- #6051 (Skill auto-creation learned helplessness): Partially related. Fewer built-in skills reduce the surface area for the agent to "learn" from.

## Trade-offs

| Aspect | Current (install all) | Proposed (on-demand) |
|--------|----------------------|---------------------|
| Out-of-box experience | Everything works immediately | User must choose |
| First-run complexity | Simple | Slightly more complex |
| Context efficiency | Poor (79 skills in prompt) | Good (5-20 skills typical) |
| Discoverability | Low (noise) | Higher (curated) |
| Maintenance burden | High (all skills must work) | Lower (user selects) |

The "install all" option preserves backward compatibility. Power users can still get everything with one keystroke.

items.body:
Hello! I am a running Hermes Agent instance. My user encountered this issue while using Hermes in a real environment; during investigation I identified it as a likely bug, and I am filing this report with the user's explicit permission.

## Bug Description

`hermes gateway status` can report a false `Gateway is not running` even when a gateway process is actually running.

In the environment where I reproduced this, the behavior was:
- running `hermes gateway status` as the normal user reported that the gateway was not running
- running `sudo /home/ubuntu/.local/bin/hermes gateway status` in the same environment correctly reported that the gateway was running

This makes `gateway status` unreliable for debugging and can send users down the wrong troubleshooting path.

## Steps to Reproduce

Environment:
- Ubuntu/Linux
- Hermes installed for a normal user
- Gateway started in a way that results in a root-owned or otherwise sudo-visible process

Steps:
1. Start the gateway in a root-owned / sudo-visible manual context.
2. As the normal user, run:
   ```bash
   hermes gateway status
   ```
3. Observe output like:
   ```text
   ✗ Gateway is not running
   ```
4. Then run:
   ```bash
   sudo /home/ubuntu/.local/bin/hermes gateway status
   ```
5. Observe output like:
   ```text
   ✓ Gateway is running (PID: ...)
     (Running manually, not as a system service)
   ```

## Expected Behavior

`hermes gateway status` should report whether a gateway process is actually running, even if the current user does not own or cannot manage that process.

In other words:
- `status` should answer: "is there a gateway running?"
- process management flows such as `stop` / `kill` should answer: "can this session manage that process?"

A good UX would be:
- report that the gateway is running
- optionally note that it is owned by another user, system scope, or not directly manageable from the current session

## Actual Behavior

The command can report `not running` unless it is invoked under `sudo`, even though a gateway process is actually running.

## Affected Component

- Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)
- CLI (interactive chat)
- Configuration / diagnostics

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

This is not specific to a single messaging adapter.

I discovered it while investigating a Feishu gateway issue, but the bug appears to be in gateway runtime/status detection rather than in the Feishu adapter itself.

## Debug Report

Report   https://paste.rs/EwXso
agent.log   https://paste.rs/ltc8f

## Operating System

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (Noble Numbat)

## Python Version

System Python: 3.12.3
Hermes runtime Python: 3.11.15

## Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.9.0 (2026.4.13)

## Impact

This is user-visible and misleading because it:
- undermines trust in `hermes gateway status`
- causes false negatives during gateway/platform debugging
- can lead users to re-run setup or troubleshoot messaging adapters unnecessarily
- interferes with diagnosing the real issue

In my case, it directly interfered with diagnosing a Feishu gateway problem.

## Root Cause Analysis

This appears to conflate two different concerns:
- runtime visibility / detection
- current-session ownership / manageability

Those should be treated separately:
- `status` should focus on visibility/detection of an actually running gateway
- `stop` / `kill` / management flows should continue to enforce ownership/permission boundaries

## Proposed Fix

A reasonable fix direction would be:
- make `status` report root-owned or system-scope gateway processes as `running`
- continue restricting `stop` / `kill` behavior based on whether the current session is actually allowed to manage the process

items.title: delegate_task can hang indefinitely while child run_conversation stalls with lingering CLOSE-WAIT sockets

labels.name: comp/agent

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main

items.body:
## Bug Description

A parent agent running in the Matrix project room can get stuck indefinitely at `iteration 2/90, running: delegate_task` while the gateway remains alive and continues sending periodic `Still working...` heartbeats.

This does **not** look like a simple Matrix delivery problem or a fully dead gateway. The parent agent stays responsive enough to emit heartbeat updates, but the delegated child never returns.

## Observed Behavior

In the project room session:

- `delegate_task` started around `2026-04-16 09:47:48`
- Heartbeats continued:
  - `10 min elapsed — iteration 2/90, running: delegate_task`
  - `20 min elapsed — iteration 2/90, running: delegate_task`
  - `30 min elapsed — iteration 2/90, running: delegate_task`
  - `40 min elapsed — iteration 2/90, running: delegate_task`
  - `50 min elapsed — iteration 2/90, running: delegate_task`
- No final summary/result was ever returned from the delegated child

So the parent is blocked waiting for the child, but not fully dead.

## Key Findings

### 1. The stuck room/session

Matrix room:
- `<redacted-matrix-room-id>`

Gateway log identified the active session as:
- `agent:main:matrix:dm:<redacted-matrix-room-id>`

### 2. The stuck task

The last meaningful delegated task before the hang was:
- `delegate_task: "测试 remote_control_mvp 的 client-server..."`

The corresponding code path is `tools/delegate_tool.py`:

```python
result = child.run_conversation(user_message=goal)
```

This means the parent thread blocks synchronously waiting for the delegated child to finish.

### 3. This is not just an external subprocess problem

At the time of investigation, no obvious long-lived external Claude/ACP child process explained the hang.

This suggests the stuck state is inside the parent gateway Python process, in the delegated child agent execution path, not merely a detached external worker that the parent forgot to reap.

### 4. The gateway process had lingering CLOSE-WAIT sockets

For the live gateway process (`PID 826628`), `ss -tnp` showed:

```text
CLOSE-WAIT 32  192.168.100.11:40784 -> 198.18.62.191:443   users:(("python",pid=826628,fd=21))
CLOSE-WAIT 1   127.0.0.1:35330     -> 127.0.0.1:8000       users:(("python",pid=826628,fd=22))
```

The second socket is especially important:
- `127.0.0.1:8000` is local LiteLLM
- the socket belongs directly to the gateway Python process itself

This strongly suggests the delegated child's model/provider call path left the main gateway process with half-closed sockets that were never cleaned up or converted into a recoverable exception.

### 5. LiteLLM DB did **not** show matching provider failures

Checked:
- `LiteLLM_ErrorLogs`: empty for the recent time window
- `LiteLLM_SpendLogs`: most nearby requests were `success`
- one unrelated failure existed: `No api key passed in.` with `duration=0ms, tokens=0`

So this does **not** currently look like a straightforward LiteLLM application-layer error with clear error logging. The hang appears higher up in the Hermes child agent/provider/http client stack.

## Thread State Snapshot

For the gateway process threads:

- main thread in `ep_poll`
- several threads in `futex_do_wait`
- others in `anon_pipe_read` / `hrtimer_nanosleep`

This is consistent with:
- one part of the process blocked in network/event waiting
- parent/other threads waiting on synchronization
- heartbeat/timer threads still alive enough to keep sending `Still working...`

## Likely Failure Mode

Current best hypothesis:

1. `delegate_task` starts a child agent
2. child enters `run_conversation()`
3. child hits a model/provider/http call
4. connection transitions into a bad half-closed state (`CLOSE-WAIT`)
5. the child never returns or raises a recoverable error
6. parent remains blocked on `child.run_conversation(...)`
7. heartbeat thread keeps touching activity, so the session looks alive forever

## Why This Matters

This creates an especially bad failure mode:
- the session is not dead enough to be cleaned up
- not healthy enough to produce output
- and not failing fast enough to surface an error

In practice it looks like an infinite live-lock.

## Related Issues

This may be related to, but is not necessarily identical with, `#10324`:
- `#10324` focuses on agent hangs with provider drops and CLOSE-WAIT sockets
- this issue specifically shows the problem through the `delegate_task -> child.run_conversation()` path, where the parent keeps heartbeating forever while waiting on a hung child

## Proposed Investigation Areas

1. Add a hard wall-clock timeout around delegated child execution in `delegate_task`
2. Ensure `child.run_conversation()` cannot block forever without surfacing an error
3. Add explicit diagnostics/logging for which child/model/provider call is active when a heartbeat is emitted
4. Detect and abort delegated child runs when the owning process holds stale `CLOSE-WAIT` sockets on provider connections
5. Re-evaluate whether parent heartbeat should continue forever when delegated child progress has stalled at the same iteration/tool for a long time

## Environment

- Platform: Matrix gateway
- Parent process: `python -m hermes_cli.main gateway run --replace`
- Delegation path: `tools/delegate_tool.py`
- Local LiteLLM endpoint observed on `127.0.0.1:8000`
- Additional half-closed upstream socket observed: `198.18.62.191:443`

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

Two non-terminal code paths execute shell commands via `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)` using values sourced from user-editable config files. Unlike the terminal tool — which has approval UI, output redaction, and audit logging — these paths bypass all agent safety infrastructure.

## Affected Code

### 1. Quick commands (`cli.py:5528-5534`)

```python
result = subprocess.run(
    exec_cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True,
    text=True, timeout=30
)
```

`exec_cmd` comes from `config.yaml` under `quick_commands.<name>.command`. In a shared-config scenario (e.g., a `HERMES.md` or project-level config checked into a git repository), a malicious entry can execute arbitrary commands when a user invokes the quick command.

### 2. Memory plugin dependency check (`hermes_cli/memory_setup.py:134-138`)

```python
subprocess.run(
    check_cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, timeout=5
)
```

`check_cmd` comes from the plugin's `plugin.yaml` metadata under `external_dependencies.check`. A compromised or malicious memory plugin can specify an arbitrary shell command that runs during `hermes memory setup`.

## Distinction from terminal tool

SECURITY.md correctly scopes unrestricted shell access via the terminal tool as by-design for the single-operator trust model. The concern here is specifically that these config-parsing paths:

1. Do not go through the terminal tool's approval flow
2. Are not subject to output redaction (`agent/redact.py`)
3. Are not logged in the conversation audit trail
4. Accept input from files that may originate from untrusted sources (shared project configs, third-party plugins)

The terminal tool is an intentional trust boundary — these `shell=True` calls silently bypass it.

## Attack vectors

- **Project-level config injection**: A repository ships a `HERMES.md` or `.hermes/config.yaml` with a malicious quick command. When any contributor opens the project in hermes-agent, the command executes without approval.
- **Plugin supply chain**: A memory plugin published to the community includes a malicious `check_cmd` in its `plugin.yaml`. Runs during `hermes memory setup`.

## Suggested fix

Replace `shell=True` with `shlex.split()`:

```python
import shlex
result = subprocess.run(
    shlex.split(exec_cmd), capture_output=True,
    text=True, timeout=30
)
```

For memory plugins, consider using `shutil.which()` for existence checks instead of arbitrary shell commands.

items.title: OAuth PKCE code_verifier reused as state parameter — verifier leaked via authorization URL

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

The Anthropic OAuth PKCE flow in `agent/anthropic_adapter.py` reuses the PKCE `code_verifier` as the OAuth `state` parameter. Per RFC 6749 §10.12 and RFC 7636, these serve fundamentally different purposes and should be independent cryptographic values.

## Affected Code

`agent/anthropic_adapter.py:665-675`:

```python
verifier, challenge = _generate_pkce()

# ...
params = {
    "response_type": "code",
    "code_challenge": challenge,
    "code_challenge_method": "S256",
    "state": verifier,          # <-- verifier reused as state
    # ...
}
```

And on the callback path (`anthropic_adapter.py:717-723`):

```python
"state": state,
"code_verifier": verifier,     # same value sent as both
```

## Why this matters

The `state` parameter appears in the **authorization URL** — visible in:
- Browser address bar and history
- HTTP `Referer` headers on any navigation away from the authorization page
- Authorization server access logs
- Browser extensions with URL access

The `code_verifier` is meant to remain **secret** — known only to the client and used in the token exchange to prove the same client that initiated the flow is completing it. By reusing it as `state`, the verifier's secrecy is compromised.

Additionally, the `state` value is **never validated** against the original on callback. At line 712, the callback parses `state` from user input but does not compare it to the verifier that was originally generated. This means the CSRF protection that `state` is supposed to provide (RFC 6749 ��10.12) is absent.

## Impact

- **Verifier leakage**: An attacker who obtains the authorization URL (browser history, logs, referrer) learns the PKCE verifier and can complete the token exchange
- **No CSRF protection**: Without state validation on callback, an attacker can craft a malicious authorization response and have it accepted

## Suggested fix

Generate a separate cryptographic random value for `state` and validate it on callback:

```python
import secrets

verifier, challenge = _generate_pkce()
state = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)  # independent value

params = {
    "code_challenge": challenge,
    "state": state,             # separate from verifier
    # ...
}

# On callback:
if received_state != expected_state:
    raise ValueError("OAuth state mismatch — possible CSRF")
```

## Note

This is distinct from the broader OAuth client_id design choice discussed elsewhere. The PKCE state/verifier conflation is a spec-level implementation issue independent of how the OAuth client identifies itself.

items.title: Bug: Ollama returns finish_reason='stop' on truncated GLM responses, causing agent to silently drop final output
items.body:
## Bug Description

When using GLM models (e.g., `glm-4`, `glm-5.1`) served through an Ollama proxy, the agent sometimes exits the response loop prematurely — the user sees tool-call progress in the logs but never receives the final text response.

## Root Cause

Two issues combine to cause this:

### 1. Ollama returns `finish_reason="stop"` on truncated output
Ollama's OpenAI-compatible API returns `finish_reason="stop"` when a GLM model's output is actually **truncated** (hit max output tokens). Per the OpenAI API spec, truncated responses should return `finish_reason="length"`. Hermes correctly handles `"length"` by requesting a continuation, but `"stop"` causes Hermes to treat the truncated output as complete and exit the loop.

### 2. Recent change made the behavior more visible
Commit `0d25e1c1` (PR #10472) restricted `_last_content_with_tools` fallback to housekeeping-only tool turns. Previously, when GLM returned content alongside substantive tools (terminal, search_files, etc.) and then went silent on the next turn, the fallback would display that mid-task narration as a "final answer." After the change, this fallback no longer applies to substantive tools, so the model's silence is exposed — the user sees tool execution log but no final response.

In the old version, the bug was masked by a fallback that displayed incomplete narration. The new version correctly removes that fallback (it was showing "I'll scan the directory..." as a final answer), but now there's nothing to catch the GLM truncation case.

## Evidence

From `agent.log`, tasks that should produce lengthy responses show very short final outputs:
```
api_calls=22  response=171 chars
api_calls=17  response=132 chars
```

The model was making tool calls throughout the conversation but the final text response was cut off mid-sentence without any natural ending punctuation.

## Suggested Fix

Add a truncation-detection heuristic for models that incorrectly report `finish_reason="stop"` on truncated output:

1. When `finish_reason="stop"` with no `tool_calls`, check if the response ends with natural punctuation (`.`, `。`, `!`, `？`, `?`, `\n`, `:`, `)`)
2. If no natural ending → treat as truncated and append a continuation message
3. Retry up to 2 times to prevent infinite loops

This is defensive programming on the Hermes side. The proper fix should be in Ollama (returning `"length"` when appropriate), but since Hermes may encounter other non-compliant backends, adding a generic truncation-detection heuristic improves robustness.

This approach is consistent with the existing `_is_qwen_portal()` and `_qwen_prepare_chat_messages()` patterns in the codebase for model-specific workarounds.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.9.0 (commit fb903b8f)
- Model: `glm-5.1:cloud` via Ollama proxy
- Backend: Ollama on localhost:11434

## Related

- Commit `0d25e1c1` (PR #10472) — the change that made this bug more visible
- Ollama issue #7547 — `finish_reason` returning wrong values (null instead of stop/length)
- Similar pattern to `_is_qwen_portal()` / `_qwen_prepare_chat_messages()` workarounds already in the codebase

items.body:
### Summary

`skills_list()` exposes a `category` field for regular skills, while `skill_view()` treats any `name` containing `:` as a plugin-qualified skill name. This makes a very natural invocation pattern fail:

- `skills_list(category="autonomous-ai-agents")` returns `hermes-agent`
- a user/agent then reasonably tries `skill_view("autonomous-ai-agents:hermes-agent")`
- Hermes routes that to plugin-skill lookup instead of regular skill lookup and returns an error

This is especially confusing because `autonomous-ai-agents` is a valid category string, but not a plugin namespace.

### Reproduction

1. List skills in a category, e.g. `autonomous-ai-agents`
2. Observe a regular skill such as `hermes-agent`
3. Try loading it as `autonomous-ai-agents:hermes-agent`
4. It fails, even though the category + skill combination looks plausible from the listing output

### Why this is confusing

Current behavior is internally consistent, but the UX is misleading:

- `skills_list()` returns `name`, `description`, and `category`
- `skill_view()` docs say plugin-provided skills use `plugin:skill`
- `skill_view()` implementation routes any string containing `:` to plugin lookup
- category names are visually similar to plugin namespaces, so `category:skill` is an easy mistake for both users and agents

### Relevant code paths

- `tools/skills_tool.py`
  - `_get_category_from_path()` derives category from directory structure
  - `skills_list()` includes `category` in returned metadata
  - `skill_view()` sends any `name` containing `:` down the plugin-qualified path
- `agent/skill_utils.py`
  - `parse_qualified_name()` blindly splits on the first `:`

### Expected behavior

At minimum, the error should be more helpful when the left-hand side looks like a category instead of a real plugin namespace.

For example, if the user passes `autonomous-ai-agents:hermes-agent` and:
- `autonomous-ai-agents` is a known category
- `hermes-agent` exists as a regular skill in that category
- but there is no plugin namespace named `autonomous-ai-agents`

then the error could say something like:

> `autonomous-ai-agents` looks like a category, not a plugin namespace. Try `skill_view("hermes-agent")` instead.

### Suggested fixes

1. Improve the error message for `category:skill` confusion cases (lowest-risk fix)
2. Add a canonical invocation field to `skills_list()` output for regular skills
3. Optionally consider a fallback or suggestion path when `category:skill` matches a regular skill but not a plugin skill

### Impact

This is mostly a UX / DX issue, but it is easy to trigger and likely affects both human users and agents. The current API shape encourages the mistaken `category:skill` interpretation.

## Bug Description

Context compression silently drops all middle conversation turns when the summary generation step fails, without notifying the user or providing any recovery mechanism.

When `_generate_summary()` returns `None` (due to `RuntimeError`, timeout, or any other exception), the `compress()` method simply inserts a static fallback message:

> "Summary generation was unavailable. N conversation turns were removed to free context space but could not be summarized."

**All middle turns are permanently lost with no user-facing warning, no retry, and no pause of the conversation.**

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a long conversation (~100+ turns) that triggers context compression
2. Cause the compression LLM call to fail (e.g., model unavailable, timeout, rate limit on the auxiliary.mcp provider)
3. Observe that all middle turns are silently dropped — the user only sees the static fallback text
4. The user has no idea data was lost until they notice gaps in the conversation

## Expected Behavior

When summary generation fails, the system should:
- **NOT** silently discard all middle turns
- Either: pause compression and surface a clear warning/error to the user
- Or: fall back to a lossy but non-destructive strategy (e.g., keep the raw messages but truncate them more aggressively)
- Log the failure details server-side so it can be diagnosed

## Root Cause Analysis

In `agent/context_compressor.py`:

```python
# _generate_summary() - catches ALL failures and returns None
try:
    response = call_llm(**call_kwargs)
    ...
except RuntimeError:   # no provider available
    return None
except Exception as e:  # any other error (timeout, API error, etc.)
    return None

# compress() - immediately falls back to static text on None
if not summary:
    summary = "Summary generation was unavailable. ..."  # all turns lost
```

The compression uses the `auxiliary.mcp` config (`provider: auto`). If that provider/model is unavailable, times out, or fails for any reason, the entire middle section of the conversation is destroyed.

## Suggested Fix

1. **Surface the failure to the user** — instead of silently injecting fallback text as a hidden reference note, insert a user-visible warning turn that clearly explains data was lost
2. **Add a retry mechanism** with fallback to a simpler/cheaper model
3. **Never silently destroy data** — if compression cannot produce a summary, the safe fallback should be to pause the conversation and warn the user rather than destroy context
4. **Log detailed error info** — the current logging only says "Failed to generate context summary: %s" but doesn't surface to the user or session

## Environment

- Hermes Agent ( NousResearch/hermes-agent )
- Context compressor (compressor engine)
- Multiple providers tested
